## Guided Tutorial 8.3: Testing Journal Entries for Management Override

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will test every journal entry of fiscal 2024 through 2026 for the characteristics in @tbl-08-03. You will bring each approver's authority limit onto the entries, add a flag for each characteristic, and combine the flags into a risk score. You will then separate the patterns that have an ordinary explanation from the entries that need follow-up, trace the highest-scoring entry to its ledger lines, and complete the workpaper.

**Prerequisites.** You need the AuditAnalytics.xlsx workbook from Tutorial 8.2.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Import the journal entries with their creators and approvers.**

a. Choose **Data > Get Data > From File > From Excel Workbook**, select CharlesRiver.xlsx, and select the **T2_JournalEntry**, **T74_Employee**, and **T1_Account** Tables. Click **Transform Data**.
b. Rename the queries `JournalEntries`, `Employees`, and `Accounts`. In Employees, keep EmployeeID, EmployeeName, JobTitle, and MaxApprovalAmount. In Accounts, keep AccountID, AccountNumber, and AccountName. Clear **Enable Load** for both.
c. In JournalEntries, set the type of PostingDate to **Date**, and of CreatedDate and ApprovedDate to **Date/Time**.
d. Merge JournalEntries with **Employees**, matching ApprovedByEmployeeID with EmployeeID. Expand EmployeeName, JobTitle, and MaxApprovalAmount, and rename them `ApproverName`, `ApproverTitle`, and `ApproverLimit`.
e. Merge JournalEntries with **Employees** again, matching CreatedByEmployeeID with EmployeeID. Expand EmployeeName and JobTitle, and rename them `CreatorName` and `CreatorTitle`.
f. Choose **Home > Close & Load**.

The JournalEntries Table holds several hundred entries, each with the names of the people who created and approved it and the approver's limit.

**Step 2. Add the five flags.** Each flag is a calculated column that returns TRUE when the entry has the characteristic.

a. Add the five columns in @tbl-08-04 to the right of the JournalEntries Table, one at a time.
b. Check a few rows by hand. For example, an entry whose CreatedByEmployeeID equals its ApprovedByEmployeeID should show TRUE in SelfApproved.

| Column | Formula |
|---|---|
| `Weekend` | `=WEEKDAY([@CreatedDate],2)>5` |
| `Backdated` | `=INT([@CreatedDate])>[@PostingDate]` |
| `SelfApproved` | `=[@CreatedByEmployeeID]=[@ApprovedByEmployeeID]` |
| `AboveLimit` | `=[@TotalAmount]>[@ApproverLimit]` |
| `RoundAmount` | `=MOD([@TotalAmount],1000)=0` |

: The flag columns of the JournalEntries Table {#tbl-08-04}

WEEKDAY with the second argument 2 numbers the days from Monday (1) to Sunday (7), so values above 5 are Saturdays and Sundays. INT removes the time from CreatedDate, so Backdated is TRUE for an entry created on a later day than the date it posts to. ApproverLimit is the approver's MaxApprovalAmount, and RoundAmount is TRUE for totals in exact thousands.

**Step 3. Combine the flags into a risk score.**

a. Add a column named `RiskScore` with this formula, which adds the five flags because Excel counts TRUE as 1 in arithmetic:

   ```
   =[@Weekend]+[@Backdated]+[@SelfApproved]+[@AboveLimit]+[@RoundAmount]
   ```

b. Add a worksheet named `JE Summary`. In A1:A5, type the five flag names, and in B1 enter `=COUNTIF(JournalEntries[Weekend],TRUE)`, with the matching column in B2:B5.
c. In A8:A13, type the scores 0 to 5, and in B8 enter `=COUNTIF(JournalEntries[RiskScore],A8)`, copied down to B13.

Most entries score 0. About two dozen have one flag, a handful have two, and a single entry has four.

**Step 4. Separate the expected patterns.** Some flags follow from how Charles River's accounting works, and a PivotTable groups them so that you can explain each pattern once.

a. Insert a PivotTable from the JournalEntries Table on a new worksheet, with CreatorTitle and EntryType in the **Rows** area and Count of EntryNumber in the **Values** area.
b. Insert a second PivotTable with EntryType in the **Rows** area, RiskScore in the **Columns** area, and Count of EntryNumber in the **Values** area.

The first PivotTable answers the question of who makes journal entries. The accounting manager creates most of them, the controller creates the monthly depreciation and the year-end closes, the production manager creates a monthly factory overhead entry, and the chief financial officer has created exactly one entry, the opening balance entry. The second PivotTable shows that some flags come in groups. Every Depreciation entry with a Weekend flag was created on the last day of a month that fell on a weekend, the date it posts to. The year-end closing entries all exceed their approver's limit, because a closing entry carries a whole year's revenue and expenses, and no employee has an approval limit above $250,000. That is a gap in the approval policy to report, not a sign of override in itself.

**Step 5. Record a disposition for each flagged entry.**

a. Sort the JournalEntries Table by RiskScore from largest to smallest, as in @fig-08-07.
b. Filter RiskScore to values of 1 or more. Copy the visible rows of the EntryNumber through RiskScore columns, and paste them on a new worksheet named `Dispositions` with **Paste Special > Values**. Clear the filter.
c. On the Dispositions worksheet, add a `Disposition` column, and type a disposition for every entry: expected, with the evidence that explains it, or follow up, with the question to ask.

Pasting values freezes the list of exceptions as evidence of what the test found, and it keeps each disposition beside its entry: text typed next to a query's output can end up beside a different row when the query is refreshed. The entries to follow up stand out in @fig-08-07. The opening balance entry has four flags: it was created by the chief financial officer on a Saturday, five days after the date it posts to, approved under the same employee ID, and far above that approver's limit. Five other entries were created on the same kind of Saturday in the first week of January, after the date they post to. The accounting manager approved several rent entries and a utilities entry that the same person had created, and the two round debt reclassifications exceed the controller's limit.

![Journal Entries Sorted by Risk Score.](/visuals/svg/fig-08-07-journal-entry-flags.svg){#fig-08-07 fig-alt="A mock of the JournalEntries Table sorted by RiskScore, with the RiskScore formula in the formula bar. It shows the entries that score two or more, with their entry number, entry type, total amount, the five flags as TRUE or FALSE, and the score. The first row, outlined, is the opening balance entry, with four flags. The entries that follow score two: a rent entry and four debt principal and interest entries, flagged as created on a weekend and backdated, and two debt reclassifications, flagged as above the approver's limit and round amounts."}

**Step 6. Trace the highest-scoring entry to the ledger.** The JournalEntry Table holds each entry's header; its lines are in GLEntry.

a. Import the **T3_GLEntry** Table, name the query `JournalLines`, and filter SourceDocumentType to JournalEntry as the first step.
b. Merge JournalLines with **Accounts** on AccountID, and expand AccountNumber and AccountName.
c. Use **Home > Choose Columns** to keep VoucherNumber, AccountNumber, AccountName, Debit, and Credit, and drag the column headers into that order. Choose **Close & Load**.
d. On the JE Summary worksheet, enter these two totals in free cells and compare them:

   ```
   =SUM(JournalEntries[TotalAmount])
   =SUM(JournalLines[Debit])
   ```

   The two totals agree, so the entries' headers and their ledger lines describe the same population.
e. Add a worksheet named `Drilldown`. In A1, type `Entry number`, and in B1 type `JE-2024-000001`. Type the headers in A3:D3 shown in @fig-08-08, and in A4 enter:

   ```
   =FILTER(JournalLines[[AccountNumber]:[Credit]],JournalLines[VoucherNumber]=B1)
   ```

The formula spills the entry's eighteen lines, the opening balances of Charles River's balance sheet, as @fig-08-08 shows. One of them is the debit to 1020 Accounts Receivable that you could not match to any invoice in Tutorial 8.2. Two independent tests, the reconciliation of the receivables and the test of the journal entries, have led to the same entry, and that makes the finding stronger. Type any other entry number in B1 to see its lines.

![The Ledger Lines of the Opening Balance Entry.](/visuals/svg/fig-08-08-journal-entry-drilldown.svg){#fig-08-08 fig-alt="A mock of the Drilldown worksheet, with the FILTER formula of cell A4 in the formula bar and the entry number JE-2024-000001 in B1. Eighteen spilled rows list the account number, account name, debit, and credit of each ledger line of the entry: cash, accounts receivable, inventories, prepaid expenses, and equipment on the debit side; accounts payable, accruals, accumulated depreciation, common stock, and retained earnings on the credit side. The accounts receivable line is outlined."}

**Step 7. Complete the workpaper.**

a. Add a worksheet named `WP Journals`, and complete the workpaper items shown in @fig-08-09.
b. In the Exceptions and disposition entry, summarize the Dispositions worksheet: the patterns that are expected and the evidence for them, and the entries to follow up.
c. Write a conclusion that says what the tests found and what remains open, and save the workbook.

![A Workpaper for the Journal Entry Tests.](/visuals/svg/fig-08-09-audit-workpaper.svg){#fig-08-09 fig-alt="A mock of the WP Journals worksheet, with workpaper labels in the first column and entries in the second: the objective, based on AS 2401; the source tables; the population check, which agrees the entries' totals with their ledger lines; the procedure, with the five flags and the risk score; the parameters of each flag; the results, as the number of entries with one, two, and four flags; the exceptions and their dispositions; the conclusion, which leaves the approval of opening and recurring entries open for follow-up; and blanks for the preparer and the reviewer."}

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the five flag columns and RiskScore calculate for every entry, and only one entry scores 4;
- the PivotTables explain the weekend depreciation entries and the year-end closes;
- the Dispositions worksheet holds a disposition for every entry with a score of 1 or more;
- the totals of the JournalEntries and JournalLines Tables agree, and the Drilldown worksheet shows the accounts receivable line of JE-2024-000001.

The journal entry tests found no sign of a concealed misstatement in the recurring entries. They did find weaknesses in how entries are approved, and they led back to the opening balance entry from two directions. That entry, created after its date, approved by its own creator, and carrying balances that the detail does not support, is the first item for the audit committee.
